title: Canary Release
shortDefinition: A gradual rollout strategy that deploys a new AI model to a small percentage of real users before full deployment.
definition: A canary release is a gradual rollout strategy where a new AI model version is deployed to a small percentage of real users first — 1%, 5%, or another defined fraction — while the existing model continues serving the remainder, allowing real-world performance to be validated at limited scale before full deployment. If the canary release reveals unexpected issues, rollback affects only the small percentage of traffic already exposed, rather than requiring emergency rollback from a full production deployment that's already reached all users.

sections.title: How canary releases limit deployment risk
sections.description: Gradually increasing traffic percentage limits the blast radius of any unexpected production issue.

content.text: By gradually increasing the traffic percentage routed to a new model version — starting small, monitoring closely, then expanding if all looks well — a canary release strategy limits the blast radius of any unexpected production issue. An unexpected problem discovered at 5% traffic exposure is far less damaging than the same problem discovered after a full deployment reaching 100% of users simultaneously, and rollback from a canary is faster and simpler than emergency full rollback from a complete deployment.

items: Start small — expose new model to limited traffic first.
Monitor closely — observe performance before expanding.
Expand gradually — increase traffic when metrics confirm quality.
Limited blast radius — issues affect only a small subset of users.
Faster rollback — simpler to revert than full deployment.

sections.title: Canary release vs. shadow deployment: choosing the right strategy

content.text: Canary release and shadow deployment address related but distinct concerns. Shadow deployment (running a new model in parallel without surfacing outputs to users) is appropriate when any real user exposure to unvalidated outputs is unacceptable. A canary release is the next step — used once shadow testing has established sufficient confidence that a small percentage of real users can be exposed to the new model's actual outputs, with close monitoring before expanding to full traffic. Most robust deployment processes use both sequentially: shadow testing first, then canary release once shadow validation is passed.

content.title: Progressive validation
content.text: Most robust deployment processes use both sequentially: shadow testing first (zero user impact), then canary release with real user exposure at limited scale.

sections.title: Limitations and risks of canary releases

content.text: Canary releases have limitations. They require robust traffic routing and monitoring infrastructure. The approach only protects against issues that manifest in the canary traffic subset — some problems may only emerge at higher traffic volumes. Canary releases add deployment complexity and time compared to full deployments. Defining appropriate promotion criteria requires careful consideration, and automated rollback thresholds must be calibrated to avoid false triggers. Canary releases don't eliminate the need for thorough staging testing before any production deployment.

items: Infrastructure requirements — needs robust traffic routing.
Scalability gap — some issues only appear at higher traffic.
Deployment complexity — adds time and process overhead.
Promotion criteria — requires careful metric definition.
False trigger risk — rollback thresholds must be calibrated.
Not a substitute — doesn't replace staging testing.

content.title: Important
content.text: Canary releases reduce but don't eliminate deployment risk. Combine with staging testing, shadow deployment, and robust monitoring for comprehensive protection.

sections.title: Best practices for canary release implementation

content.text: Implementing canary releases effectively requires careful metric definition, automation, and risk-calibrated thresholds. The following practices can help ensure your canary releases provide reliable risk protection.

content.title: Recommended approach:
items: Define clear promotion criteria before the release begins.
Start with small traffic percentages (1-5%) for initial exposure.
Set up automated rollback triggers for key metric degradation.
Monitor both model-specific and infrastructure metrics.
Calibrate thresholds to avoid false triggers.
Use shadow deployment before canary for consequential models.
Document canary release decisions and outcomes.
Consider manual approval for high-stakes model updates.

content.title: Key metric
content.text: Measure canary success rate — what percentage of canary releases successfully progress to full deployment? Low rates may indicate overly aggressive promotion criteria or model quality issues.

faqs.title: Frequently asked questions about canary releases

items.question: What percentage of traffic should start a canary release?
items.answer: This depends on your specific risk tolerance and user volume; typical starting points range from 1–10%, though the right number depends on how many affected users even a small percentage represents at your scale.

items.question: How is a canary release different from an A/B test?
items.answer: They're closely related — a canary release specifically focuses on safely validating a new model version before full rollout; an A/B test is typically run longer to measure business impact differences between model versions rather than primarily as a deployment safety mechanism.

items.question: Should we always run shadow deployment before a canary release?
items.answer: For consequential AI systems, yes — shadow deployment validates real production behavior without any user exposure, making canary releases safer by starting from an already-validated baseline.

items.question: Can canary releases be automated, or do they require manual promotion decisions?
items.answer: Both are possible; ClickMasters builds automated promotion with pre-defined metric thresholds for routine, lower-stakes model updates, and recommends human review before expanding traffic for updates to more consequential systems.

items.question: How long does a canary release typically run before full promotion?
items.answer: Long enough to observe sufficient traffic volume and diversity to be confident the new model is behaving consistently; ClickMasters defines minimum volume and time thresholds based on your specific system's risk profile.

items.question: How long does building canary release infrastructure take?
items.answer: 8–22 weeks depending on automation requirements and whether a full shadow-plus-canary pipeline is included.

items.question: What is the difference between a canary release and a blue-green deployment?
items.answer: Blue-green deployment runs two identical environments and switches traffic at once. Canary release gradually shifts traffic in increments. Canary provides more granular validation and lower risk for AI model updates.

items.question: How do you monitor a canary release for AI models?
items.answer: Monitor both system metrics (latency, error rates) and AI-specific metrics (accuracy, prediction distribution, confidence scores). ClickMasters builds comprehensive monitoring calibrated to your AI system's risk indicators.

items.question: What are common promotion criteria for canary releases?
items.answer: Common criteria include: error rates within acceptable thresholds, latency within bounds, model accuracy meeting targets, and no significant changes in prediction distribution over a defined period with sufficient traffic volume.

items.question: Can canary releases be used for LLM-based applications?
items.answer: Yes — canary releases are valuable for LLM applications when updating prompts, model versions, or RAG configurations. Gradual rollout allows validation before full user exposure.
